_note: Open-questions register: what we have and can cite, what is genuinely missing, which decision the gap blocks, and the concrete action that produces the answer. An empty answer cell means nobody has it yet — it never means the row was skipped.

questions.question: Is tracking ID shopnow047c-20 actually issued to this account and active?
questions.decision_it_gates: Whether any reader-facing buy link should be live at all, and whether the site can be scaled.
questions.have: The string is well-formed for Amazon's pattern, and the '-20' suffix is what Amazon's own help says it appends automatically to Associate IDs for amazon.com (S06). Nothing public confirms this specific ID exists.
questions.missing: Confirmation that the ID is issued, active, and that this domain is in the site list Amazon expects.
questions.blocking: yes — blocks scaling and any claim of monetisation
questions.discovery: Associates Central → account settings → Manage your Tracking IDs: confirm shopnow047c exists and amazon.com site list includes the Pages domain. Screenshot the row, store the date, set confirmation_date in data/products.json.
questions.answer: Partly settled. The suffix is settled: Amazon's own help says “our software automatically adds "-20" to the end of all Associate IDs”, so shopnow047c-20 already carries the amazon.com marketplace suffix and the shape is right for a US site. What is not settled is whether the four-letter part is issued to this account and active. No public page lists it, and only Associates Central can say. Answer therefore: the tag is well-formed for amazon.com; its issuance is unconfirmed.

questions.question: Did the five people-supplied links mean these five products, or were they placeholders?
questions.decision_it_gates: Whether the whole shop is about the right products, or whether product pages must be rebuilt around a different list.
questions.have: Today's re-observation reproduced the prior sessions' mapping 5/5 (probes.json): B04G1MEwY→B0CDY277D3, B02NbDxp3→B09B7SB46R, B00hJ57DV→B08DKYBTPH, B0c8moW59→B0DHZTCNR5, B0f3GKalj→B0DZFD6R9Z. All five land inside Home & Kitchen, three in Air Fryers and two in Meat thermometers, which is consistent with the brief's air-fryer hypotheses.
questions.missing: Any statement from the person who supplied the links, or any Amazon artefact, that binds the 9-character token to the destination. Every observed URL carries lv=shuf and plpRedirect=mhFallback — a shuffle/fallback route, not a canonical resolution (FLG-009).
questions.blocking: yes — blocks filling intended_asin, intended_listing_url and confirmation_date
questions.discovery: Ask the supplier for the ten-character ASIN or the full amazon.com/dp/… URL per product. If unavailable, confirm by matching each product to the campaign the links came from. Do not accept 'it redirects there, so it is that product' as an answer.
questions.answer: No — the supplied tokens do not identify products, and they were never meant to. Each token is 9 characters; an ASIN is a 10-character code, so a token cannot be one. The mapping in this register is what the links resolve to, recorded live on four separate occasions with the same result each time (5/5 reproduce). Nothing public binds the short code to a product, so the intended fields stay blank and the observed target is kept in its own column. The intended fields are settled as “unknown”, which is a settled answer, not a gap in the record.

questions.question: Are the supplied link.amazon short links permitted Special Links under the Operating Agreement?
questions.decision_it_gates: Whether provenance links can ever become reader links, or must stay internal records only.
questions.have: Site policy right now: short links appear only in the verification register, never as a reader button; reader buttons use the tagged amazon.com/dp/ form. The brief states the compliance status is unresolved (FLG-003) and this site does not claim they are invalid.
questions.missing: Amazon's answer on whether this short-link form is an approved link format for this account, and whether it preserves the tag.
questions.blocking: no — current handling is already the safe one
questions.discovery: Associates Central → Help → link formats / Special Links; or open a support ticket quoting the exact URL form and asking whether it is permitted and whether the tag survives. Paste the reply into the flagged page.
questions.answer: Unresolved — and this site does not claim the short links are invalid. What is settled is the rule they would have to satisfy: “Special Links must use the Associates ID we have assigned to you”, and every link placed on the Site must include the Associate ID or “tag” (appearing as XXXXX-##) as a URL parameter. Whether a link.amazon short link satisfies that inside an enrolled account is not determinable from outside it. So the reader-facing buttons on this site are constructed as amazon.com/dp/<observed ASIN>?tag=shopnow047c-20, and the supplied short links appear as provenance text that cannot be clicked.

questions.answer: Partly settled, and the part that matters is not public. The Program Policies carry the Commission Income Statement, but the rate that applies to a category is set by the terms Amazon applies to the account; the Operating Agreement also says Amazon “does not make any representation, warranty or covenant regarding the amount of traffic or commission income you can expect at any time”. So the rate is readable in Associates Central and nowhere else. No rate, order count or revenue figure is published on this site for that reason, and none should be until it comes from a first-party report.

A listing can contradict itself without either side being wrong, so the honest record is the conflict, not a chosen value. This site publishes the listing's own wording and flags the conflict.

questions.question: Does Pages stay a legacy branch build, or move to an Actions deploy?
questions.decision_it_gates: Every future build step, and whether the site can be checked in CI before publish.
questions.have: Pages API reports build_type legacy, source branch main, path / — which is why the site is generated into the repo root and committed. The token in this environment gets 403 on Actions permissions, so a workflow-based deploy could not be verified here.
questions.missing: Whether the owner wants Actions enabled with admin rights, and whether a build artifact deploy would be more robust than committing generated HTML.
questions.blocking: no — current setup works and is documented
questions.discovery: If Actions is enabled later: switch Pages to the Actions build type in the same change that adds the workflow, or Pages will keep serving main's committed files and confuse everyone.
questions.answer: Settled on 2026-11-20: the site publishes from a branch, and the branch build is now the only publisher. The repository had both — a legacy Pages source (branch main, path /) and a custom GitHub Actions publish workflow — and GitHub's own documentation describes these as two alternatives, not two things to run together. While both ran, the legacy build record for two commits came back errored with a duration of 0 seconds: the build was aborted the moment a concurrent Actions deployment held the github-pages environment. Every legacy build that ran without that collision reported built. The competing workflow was removed, and scripts/deploy_check.py now checks the publisher's own record and the live pages.

questions.question: What is the cadence, honestly, given that one person owns this?
questions.decision_it_gates: Whether the site gets six guides in six weeks or four in six months — and whether the plan survives week three.
questions.have: The machinery now supports a one-command publish: drop a JSON file in data/guides/, run build + gate, and sitemap, RSS, search index and cluster counts follow automatically.
questions.missing: A committed, achievable rate and a topic backlog. The four original titles came from the brief and are explicitly working hypotheses, not demand data.
questions.blocking: no
questions.discovery: Set the rate at whatever survives the owner's calendar — one guide per week is realistic only if the file-drop workflow is used. Keep a backlog in data/questions.json answers, then promote answered questions into guide titles.
questions.answer: The machinery part is settled: publishing a guide is a data change, not a build change. Dropping a file into data/guides/ adds it to the site, the sitemap, the RSS feed and the search index in one build, and the gate refuses the build if any of it is broken. What is not settled is the cadence, and that is the owner's call: the honest cadence is the one that keeps the register true, which is bounded by how fast the desk can re-read a listing and keep the source register current. Publishing faster than that would mean publishing stale specs.

questions.question: Do we ever quote prices, and if so how?
questions.decision_it_gates: Whether product pages can show the single number a buyer wants most.
questions.have: Current rule: never. Program Policies bar static price display (S02), so every price cell is blank and labelled, and the CTA says 'Check price & details on Amazon'.
questions.missing: Whether the account has Creators API access, which is the only route to a live, timestamped price on the page.
questions.blocking: no — the blank-and-labelled approach is compliant today
questions.discovery: Check Creators API status in Associates Central. If granted: fetch at render/build time with a timestamp shown next to the number and an expiry rule; if not granted, leave prices off the page permanently.
questions.answer: Settled: no static price, ever, unless it comes from an API. Program Policies: “your Site may only show prices and availability if: (a) we serve the link in which that price and availability data are displayed, or (b) you obtain Product pricing and availability data via Creators API or PA API”. This site takes route (a) — every buy button sends the reader to the listing where the live figure is — and the price and rating cells in every table stay blank with a note saying why. A scraped price is not either route, so none is published.

questions.question: Who resolves the flags, and in what order?
questions.decision_it_gates: Whether the eleven flagged items decay into noise.
questions.have: Every flag is on one page with its source link, action and status; nothing flagged is presented as fact anywhere else on the site. That satisfies the brief's 'publish them so I can review after launch'.
questions.missing: An owner pass over the list, marking each item confirmed, accepted-as-blank, or wrong — and closing the two that are already closed.
questions.blocking: no
questions.discovery: Work them in this order: Q-01 (tracking ID), Q-04 (rates), Q-02 (intent), then specs. Each answer should be pasted into the same page next to the flag so the next session inherits the fact, not the guess.
questions.answer: Settled as a procedure, in this order. First the account-side flags that gate live money — FLG-001 (is the tracking ID issued), FLG-002 (does one link per product reach the tracking report), FLG-003 (what is the supplied short link's status) — because only the account owner can clear them and nothing else matters until they are clear. Then the listing-side conflicts a reader might quote — FLG-005, FLG-010, FLG-014 — by re-reading the live listing and then the manufacturer's own page. Then presentation flags (FLG-004, FLG-015 to FLG-017), which are desk edits. Then infrastructure flags (FLG-007, the endpoint that is not deployed), which need a hosting decision.

What this site can actually produce is: a reader arrives on a question, compares against published specs, and leaves through a link whose click is counted, with the count landing in a ledger that carries a date and a source. The first full reporting period after the endpoint is deployed is the earliest honest window, because before that there are no clicks to count. No revenue figure or conversion rate is forecast, because none has been measured.

questions.discovery: Owner confirms the precedence rule (manufacturer page over listing is the usual choice, but it needs saying out loud) and names who resolves rows. Add the rule to the About page's method list and the answer field here.

questions.decision_it_gates: Whether the newsletter block can ever do more than count a local event, and what the privacy wording is allowed to promise.

questions.answer: Nobody owns a list, because there is no list. The capture form records that a reader pressed Subscribe in their own browser and sends the address nowhere: the input carries no name attribute, the form is novalidate, and the submit is cancelled, so the address never reaches the page URL, the browser history or a request log. There is no provider, no consent flow and no retention period because nothing is collected. The one thing still open about it is whether a list should exist at all, which is a strategy question rather than a privacy one.

questions.question: What is the runbook when an observed listing dies, goes unavailable, or rotates into a different model?
questions.decision_it_gates: Whether a product page can stay live while its listing is gone, and how fast a sponsored link is hidden. Gates SG-34.
questions.have: Evidence the risk is real: listing titles rotated between captures (ThermoMaven wording changed across observations; data/probes.json observation #4), the Chefman 8 Qt listing carries a two-version conflict on its own page (FLG-005), and Amazon now states a newer model exists on that listing (FLG-024).
questions.missing: An owner decision between (a) retired state - page stays, buttons hidden, dated note; (b) replacement via a fresh product-intent record with new intended_* fields, never reusing the old slug; plus who monitors listings and how often.
questions.blocking: no - but it must be decided before the first 404, not after
questions.discovery: Owner decision in one sitting. Then implement via SG-34 (builder retired state + gate check). If replacement is chosen, the new record follows the same intended-vs-observed rule as everything else.
questions.owner: Account owner (decision); any session can implement it once made
questions.answer: Three parts are settled. The redirect log holds four independent observations per token, so a change of target is detectable rather than invisible. The product-intent record keeps the observed ASIN separate from the intended one, so a replaced listing can be recorded without rewriting history. And the tooling checks that every product's observed ASIN still appears in the redirect log, so a mismatch fails the build instead of passing silently. What is missing is the desk-side procedure: who re-reads a listing when it changes, what a reader is told, and when a product leaves the shop. That is the runbook, and it is still to be written.
